producer_brief.topic_summary: Specimen BP/1/5558 from the ~250 Ma Early Triassic Karoo Basin (Fernandez et al., PLOS ONE 2013): an excavated red sandstone burrow cast holding a curled mammal-relative (Thrinaxodon) beside an injured amphibian (Broomistega).
producer_brief.core_dramatic_question: Why were a carnivorous mammal-relative and a water-loving amphibian fossilized peacefully nose-to-tail inside one sun-baked desert rock?
producer_brief.target_emotion_arc: Sun-baked desert curiosity -> forensic shock at 'Wait. They were not enemies.' -> empathetic warmth for two drought refugees -> visceral awe as monsoon mud seals them for 250 million years.
producer_brief.audience_takeaway: Crushed, actively healing ribs with zero bite marks prove the injured amphibian crawled into a sleeping Thrinaxodon's cool burrow to survive scorching drought before a flash flood entombed them both.

observed_evidence: Synchrotron micro-CT of Karoo Basin burrow cast BP/1/5558 revealed articulated skeletons of Thrinaxodon liorhinus and Broomistega putterilli in direct contact.
Broomistega preserves multiple consecutive fractured ribs with bony healing calluses and zero tooth puncture marks on skull or postcrania.
scientific_inferences: Thrinaxodon was likely aestivating (dormant heat-sleep) inside its cool burrow so it did not attack the injured amphibian intruder.
A rapid high-energy overbank sediment flood filled the burrow and preserved both skeletons undisturbed.
illustrative_abstractions: Sunlit amber-calcite geological cross-section peel through the field sandstone nodule and #E63926 vermilion highlight on healing rib calluses.

anti_clone_declaration.why_not_previous_template: Eliminates the dark obsidian synchrotron room, rotating turntable pedestal, cyan neon rings, and sci-fi HUD — staging 100% outdoors in a blazing 4300K South African Karoo badlands excavation trench cross-cut with the living 250 Ma floodplain.
